title: What PCOS is
content: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition affecting people with ovaries, involving a combination of irregular periods, higher levels of androgens ("male" hormones), and/or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. It is not caused by having many cysts — the name is a historical misnomer.

title: How PCOS is diagnosed (Rotterdam criteria)
content: In adults, PCOS is diagnosed when at least 2 of these 3 features are present, after ruling out other conditions that mimic it: irregular or absent ovulation/periods, clinical or biochemical signs of excess androgens, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. This requires clinical assessment, blood tests, and often an ultrasound — it cannot be diagnosed from symptoms or a questionnaire alone.

title: Diagnosis in adolescents is stricter
content: In adolescents, both irregular periods AND clinical/biochemical signs of excess androgens are required — polycystic ovaries on ultrasound are not used to diagnose PCOS in this age group, because polycystic-appearing ovaries are common in teenagers without PCOS. This applies to teens, not just "adolescents" in clinical terms.

title: How common PCOS is
content: PCOS affects an estimated 8-13% of women of reproductive age. Up to 70% of affected women remain undiagnosed worldwide.

title: Common symptoms
content: Symptoms vary widely between individuals and can include irregular or absent periods, excess facial or body hair growth (hirsutism), acne, scalp hair thinning, weight gain, and skin darkening in body folds (acanthosis nigricans, linked to insulin resistance).

title: PCOS and fertility
content: PCOS is one of the most common causes of reduced fertility due to irregular or absent ovulation, but it does not mean infertility — most people with PCOS can conceive, often with support such as lifestyle changes, ovulation induction medication, or assisted reproduction if needed.

title: Long-term health associations
content: PCOS is associated with a higher likelihood of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and metabolic syndrome over time. These are statistical associations that support regular check-ups, not a guarantee that any individual will develop them.

title: Mental health and PCOS
content: Anxiety and depression are more common in people with PCOS than in the general population. The guideline recommends routine emotional wellbeing screening as part of PCOS care, not just physical symptom management.

title: First-line management: lifestyle
content: Healthy lifestyle habits — balanced nutrition and regular physical activity — are recommended as first-line management for PCOS, since even modest changes can improve symptoms, insulin sensitivity, and cycle regularity for many people. This is about overall health, not a specific weight target.

title: Medical treatment options
content: Depending on symptoms and goals, treatment can include combined oral contraceptives (to regulate cycles and reduce androgen effects), metformin (for insulin resistance), anti-androgen medications (for hair growth/acne), or fertility-specific treatment. The right option depends on individual goals and should be discussed with a clinician.

title: PCOS is not one-size-fits-all
content: PCOS presents differently across individuals and ethnic groups — for example, hirsutism is more visibly reported in some populations than others. Guidelines recommend individualized assessment rather than assuming a single symptom pattern applies to everyone.

title: Cause of PCOS
content: The exact cause of PCOS is not fully understood. It is thought to involve a combination of genetic and environmental factors, and often runs in families, though no single gene has been identified as the cause.

title: When to see a doctor
content: It's worth seeing a doctor about possible PCOS if you have irregular or absent periods, signs of excess androgens (such as new or worsening acne or hair growth), or difficulty conceiving. A clinician can arrange the right tests and rule out other causes that can look similar to PCOS, such as thyroid conditions.

title: Ultrasound is not required for every diagnosis
content: If irregular ovulation and clinical/biochemical excess androgens are both already present in an adult, a diagnosis can be made without an ultrasound. Ultrasound is one of three possible criteria, not a mandatory test for everyone.

title: PCOS and weight
content: Not everyone with PCOS is overweight, and not everyone who is overweight has PCOS — the relationship goes in both directions (excess weight can worsen PCOS symptoms, and PCOS's hormonal/insulin effects can make weight management harder), but body weight alone is neither required for, nor proof of, a PCOS diagnosis.
